title: Why Coordination Drifts and Eventually Reaches Its Processing Limit
summary: Coordination that once worked does not remain appropriate forever. As reality, scale, and participants change, old rules can drift away from actual conditions; as patches, exceptions, and communication needs accumulate, coordination itself can reach a saturation point.
shortAnswer: Coordination that once worked does not remain appropriate forever. As reality, scale, and participants change, old rules can drift away from actual conditions; as patches, exceptions, and communication needs accumulate, coordination itself can reach a saturation point.
displayQuestion: Why Coordination Drifts and Eventually Reaches Its Processing Limit

blocks.text: Coordination drift rarely begins with obvious failure. The original rule, process, or division of labor may have solved a real problem. What changes is the environment around it: user numbers grow, networks expand, technology shifts, member capability changes, and risk moves. Because the structure worked before, participants often keep repairing it locally rather than asking whether the assumptions that made it effective still exist.

A common signal of drift is that rules are still formally followed while outcomes increasingly depend on exceptions. More cases need manual interpretation, more roles must work around the process, and more temporary arrangements keep being renewed. This can look like healthy flexibility, but it may indicate a growing distance between formal coordination and actual reality. The more exceptions accumulate, the harder it becomes to know what the real rule is.

Drift also creates divergence in meaning. Different locations develop their own patches and local interpretations to make the old structure work. The same process begins to represent different actions across teams; the same metric begins to mean different forms of success at different levels. Coordination has not yet fragmented completely, but shared language becomes thinner, and the system increasingly depends on a few people who can translate among local realities.

As patches accumulate, the runtime approaches coordination saturation. Saturation is not merely high workload. It is the point at which the shared structure nears the limit of relationships and exceptions it can process. Meetings multiply without reducing misunderstanding, rules become more detailed while boundary disputes increase, and management intervenes more frequently without reducing temporary decisions. Additional coordination no longer lowers friction; it becomes a new source of friction.

A saturated coordination layer has little remaining margin for new reality. Each new project, participant, or risk forces the structure to delay, simplify, or ignore something else. The most reliable coordinators become bottlenecks because all exceptions need them. Output can continue while the system loses its ability to expand or absorb surprise. At this point the instruction to communicate more often can simply occupy the interfaces even further.

Repair requires distinguishing rule updates from structural reconstruction. If only a few conditions changed, adjusting the process may be enough. If many exceptions point back to the same obsolete assumption, roles, interfaces, layers, or responsibility boundaries may need redesign. Mature coordination does not endlessly add rules; it can remove coordination acts that no longer have a function and relocate complexity to a more appropriate layer.

Coordination drift therefore shows that past effectiveness is not present fit, while coordination saturation shows that coordination capacity is itself finite. A healthy structure can recover alignment after error; a saturated one leaves a long tail after every small deviation, so backlogs grow and participants increasingly rely on memory, personal relationships, and private tracking. The task becomes protecting simple, clear, scalable shared interfaces rather than preserving every existing process.

blocks.heading: Key judgment
blocks.statement: Coordination drift is the growing mismatch between inherited structure and current reality; coordination saturation is the accumulation of patches and exceptions until the processing limit is reached. Repair may require less coordination and structural redesign rather than more communication.

blocks.question: Which temporary exceptions in your current coordination have become permanent? If more meetings, rules, and communication no longer reduce friction, what old assumption or structural boundary now needs to be changed?
